name: GitHub (OAuth Apps and GitHub Apps)
summary: GitHub has no app review for going public: you can register a GitHub App (recommended) or an OAuth App in minutes and any GitHub user can connect immediately. The real friction is on your users' side: organization owners must install a GitHub App on their org, or approve an OAuth App when OAuth app access restrictions are on (the default for new orgs). Only a GitHub Marketplace listing involves a GitHub review, and paid plans additionally need a verified-publisher organization and 100+ installs.

verdict.headline: 15-45 minutes to register and test; no GitHub review to go public. Marketplace listing (optional) adds an unpublished-length review, reportedly 2-6 weeks.
verdict.rationale: Registration is self-serve at Settings > Developer settings with no verification, domain check or policy review. Making a GitHub App public is a single setting ("Any account"). The only provider-side review is the optional GitHub Marketplace listing. The practical blocker for an AI-agent product is organization access: org owners control GitHub App installation and, with OAuth app access restrictions enabled, must approve OAuth Apps before they can reach org data.

evidence.quote: any user on GitHub can install it and authorize it.
evidence.note: No review step exists in the GitHub App or OAuth App registration docs; the only review described is the Marketplace 'Request publish' flow.

effort.approvalNote: No GitHub approval is needed to register an app or make a GitHub App public. A GitHub review happens only if you submit a GitHub Marketplace listing (an onboarding expert reviews it; GitHub publishes no timeline). Separately, each customer organization's owner must install your GitHub App, or approve your OAuth App if OAuth app access restrictions are enabled; that wait depends on the customer, not GitHub.

evidence.quote: To finish your app listing submission, you can request a review by an onboarding expert.
evidence.note: Marketplace wait times are not published; see the marketplace path for the community-reported range.

paths.name: Personal / testing (private GitHub App)
paths.when: You are prototyping your agent and only you (or members of your own org) will connect.
paths.whatChanges: Register a GitHub App with "Only on this account". It can only be installed on the owning account, and only members of the owning organization can authorize it. Use localhost callback URLs or the device flow.

evidence.quote: it can only be installed on the account that owns the app.

paths.name: Public GitHub App (no Marketplace) - recommended default
paths.when: You want any GitHub user or organization to connect their account to your agent.
paths.whatChanges: Choose "Any account" under "Where can this GitHub App be installed?", add production callback URLs, a webhook secret (if webhooks are active), and a private key for installation tokens. No GitHub review. Your public app gets a landing page at github.com/apps/<slug> with an Install button. Org customers need an org owner (or repo admin) to install it.

evidence.quote: Public GitHub Apps have a landing page with an **Install** button

paths.name: OAuth App (legacy model; enterprise-level access)
paths.when: You need enterprise-object access (GitHub Apps cannot be granted enterprise permissions), or you only need 'Sign in with GitHub' plus broad user-scoped access and accept coarse scopes.
paths.whatChanges: Register under "OAuth apps". Uses coarse scopes (e.g. `repo` grants read AND write to all private repos). Org data is blocked until each org owner approves the app when OAuth app access restrictions are enabled (default for new orgs). Rate limit does not scale with installations.

evidence.quote: There is one case where an OAuth app is preferred over a GitHub App.

paths.name: GitHub Marketplace listing (free or paid)
paths.when: You want discoverability in GitHub Marketplace or want to sell plans billed through GitHub.
paths.whatChanges: App must be public, integrate beyond authentication, have a privacy policy link, support link, logo/feature card/screenshots, and Marketplace plan-change webhooks. You accept the GitHub Marketplace Developer Agreement and click "Request publish"; an onboarding expert contacts you. Paid plans additionally require an organization-owned app, publisher verification (org 2FA + verified domain), 100+ installations for a GitHub App (200+ users for an OAuth App), Marketplace purchase-event handling and monthly + annual billing.

evidence.note: Requirements are documented (s15, s16, s17). GitHub publishes no review timeline; the 2-6 week range comes from community reports aggregated by a third party and is unverified. A 2018 GitHub blog post described cutting listing time to about 2 weeks (s19), which may be outdated.

appModel.providerTerm: GitHub App (recommended) or OAuth App, registered under a personal account or organization in Developer settings
appModel.explanation: One GitHub App registration represents your agent product. Customers 'install' it on their user or org account and choose which repositories it can reach; each installation yields short-lived installation access tokens (app acting as itself). When a user 'authorizes' it, you get a user access token that can only reach resources both the user and the app installation can access. An OAuth App instead has no installation concept: each user authorization yields a scope-limited token acting as that user across everything they can see (subject to org approval).
appModel.tokenNotes: GitHub App user access tokens expire after 8 hours with a refresh token valid 6 months (option "Expire user authorization tokens", on by default; strongly recommended). Using a refresh token invalidates it and the old access token. Installation access tokens expire after 1 hour and are minted with a JWT signed by the app's private key (keys never expire; up to 25 per app). OAuth Apps now also offer expiring tokens (8h / 6-month refresh) via "Expire user access tokens", enabled by default on new registrations; otherwise OAuth tokens live until revoked. The `scope` parameter grants nothing to a GitHub App; permissions come from the app registration. Authorization codes expire after 10 minutes.

evidence.quote: The user access token expires after eight hours

requirements.detail: Register under your personal account or under an org you own (or where you are a GitHub App manager). Each account can register up to 100 GitHub Apps and up to 100 OAuth Apps. For a product, register under an organization so the app survives staff changes and is eligible for paid Marketplace plans.

evidence.quote: A user or organization can register up to 100 GitHub Apps

requirements.detail: GitHub App names must be unique across GitHub and cannot match an existing account name unless it is your own. The slug (lowercased, spaces to '-') appears in the UI when the app acts.

evidence.quote: The name cannot be longer than 34 characters.

requirements.detail: Required. If you lack a site, a public repository URL or the owning account URL is acceptable.

evidence.quote: you can use the URL of the account that owns the app.

requirements.item: Callback URL(s) (web flow) or Device Flow enabled (CLI/headless agents)
requirements.detail: Both GitHub Apps and OAuth Apps accept up to 10 callback URLs; pass `redirect_uri` to choose one, otherwise the first is used. Optional wildcard matching for subdomains/subdirectories exists but is a security risk. Headless agents should enable Device Flow (no callback or client secret needed).

evidence.quote: You can specify up to 10 callback URLs.

requirements.item: Minimum permissions (GitHub App) or scopes (OAuth App)
requirements.detail: Pick Read-only / Read & write / No access per permission. Changing permissions later forces every installation owner to re-approve, so get them right before going public.

evidence.quote: You should select the minimum permissions necessary for your app.

requirements.item: Private key (GitHub App) and client secret
requirements.detail: Generate a private key (PEM, PKCS#1) to sign JWTs for installation tokens; generate a client secret for the web flow token exchange. Store both in a secrets manager.

evidence.quote: Private keys do not expire and instead need to be manually revoked.

requirements.item: Org owner action at each customer organization
requirements.detail: GitHub App: only an org owner or repo admin can install (members can request). OAuth App: if OAuth app access restrictions are enabled, an org owner must approve the app before members' tokens can reach org resources. Restrictions are on by default for new orgs.

evidence.quote: When you create a new organization, OAuth app access restrictions are enabled by default.

requirements.detail: Publisher contact info, description, pricing plan, valid privacy policy link, support link or email, logo, feature card and screenshots, Marketplace plan-change webhooks, and value beyond authentication. Only org owners (not GitHub App managers) can submit org-owned listings.

evidence.quote: Listings must have a valid link to a privacy policy.

requirements.item: Publisher verification (paid plans or Marketplace badge only)
requirements.detail: App must be owned by an organization; org needs accurate profile and email, org-wide two-factor authentication required, and a verified domain with a 'Verified' badge on the org profile.

evidence.quote: To offer paid plans for your app or to include a marketplace badge

requirements.item: Install / user thresholds for paid plans
requirements.detail: Paid apps: GitHub Apps should have at least 100 installations; OAuth Apps at least 200 users. Must handle Marketplace purchase events (new, upgrade, downgrade, cancel, free trial) and support monthly and annual billing.

evidence.quote: GitHub Apps should have a minimum of 100 installations.

steps.title: Decide: GitHub App (default) vs OAuth App
steps.actorNote: Pure decision; an agent can apply this rubric to your product requirements.
instructions: Pick a GitHub App unless you need enterprise-level resources (the enterprise object itself), which only OAuth Apps can be granted.

GitHub App advantages for an AI agent: fine-grained permissions (e.g. read-only contents instead of `repo`), users choose specific repositories, expiring tokens, rate limits that scale with installations, a built-in webhook, and no dependency on org OAuth app policies.

Decide whether the agent acts as the user (user access token via web or device flow), as itself (installation token via private key + JWT), or both. Agents that open PRs as a bot use installation tokens; agents that act 'as you' use user access tokens.
For CLI or terminal agents without a browser redirect, plan to use the device flow.

steps.title: Fill in the New GitHub App form
steps.actorNote: An agent can draft every value (name, URLs, permission list); you paste them while logged in and click create.
instructions: "GitHub App name": unique, 34 characters max.
"Homepage URL": your product site (or repo URL).
"Callback URL": your OAuth redirect (e.g. https://yourapp.com/auth/github/callback). Click "Add callback URL" to add a localhost dev URL too (up to 10 total).

Select "Request user authorization (OAuth) during installation" if you want the install and user login to happen in one hop (this disables "Setup URL").

Webhooks: deselect "Active" if the agent does not react to events; otherwise set "Webhook URL" and a "Webhook secret" and keep SSL verification enabled.
"Permissions": set only what the agent needs (e.g. Repository > Contents: Read-only, Issues: Read & write).
"Where can this GitHub App be installed?": "Only on this account" for testing, "Any account" to let customers connect.
Click "Create GitHub App". Note the App ID and Client ID shown on the settings page.

steps.title: Implement the user authorization flow (web flow with PKCE, or device flow)
steps.actorNote: Pure code work; a coding agent can implement and unit-test this with your client ID/secret in env vars.
instructions: Web flow: redirect to https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize with client_id, redirect_uri, a random state, and PKCE code_challenge (S256 only; 'plain' unsupported). Exchange the code (valid 10 minutes) at POST https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token.

Device flow: POST https://github.com/login/device/code with client_id; show user_code and https://github.com/login/device; poll POST https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token at the returned interval (default 5s). Codes expire after 900 seconds. A slow_down error adds 5 seconds to the interval. No client secret needed.
Store refresh_token (ghr_ prefix) and expires_in (28800s). Refresh before expiry; each refresh rotates both tokens, so persist the new pair atomically.
For GitHub App bot actions: sign a JWT with the private key, then create an installation access token (1-hour lifetime) per installation.
Do not send `scope` for GitHub Apps except `offline_access`; permissions come from the app registration.

blockers.title: Users can sign in but the agent cannot see org repositories (OAuth App)
blockers.symptom: API calls for org private repos return 404/403 or empty lists; webhooks from org private repos stop arriving.
blockers.fix: The org has OAuth app access restrictions enabled (default for new orgs). Ask the user to click "Request access" for the org under Settings > Applications > Authorized OAuth Apps, and have an org owner grant access under "OAuth app policy". Long-term: switch to a GitHub App, which is not subject to org application policies.

evidence.quote: API access** to private organization resources is not available for unapproved OAuth apps.

blockers.title: GitHub App user token cannot access a repo the user clearly can
blockers.symptom: User access token returns 404 for a repo the user owns or belongs to.
blockers.fix: User access tokens only reach resources both the user and the app can access. The app must be installed on that account/org and the repo included in the installation. Send the user to https://github.com/apps/YOUR-SLUG/installations/new.

evidence.quote: can only access resources that both the user and app can access.

blockers.title: Org members cannot install your GitHub App
blockers.symptom: Non-owner members only see a 'request' option; installation stalls waiting on an org owner.
blockers.fix: Only org owners (or repo admins for their repos) can install. Give customers an owner-facing install link and explanation of the minimal permissions requested.

evidence.quote: You must be an organization owner or have admin permissions in a repository

blockers.title: Tokens suddenly invalid after 8 hours, or refresh fails
blockers.symptom: 401 Bad credentials after ~8 hours; refresh requests fail after a refresh token was already used once.
blockers.fix: Expiring tokens are on by default. Refresh with grant_type=refresh_token before expiry and atomically persist the new access + refresh token; each refresh token is single-use. Refresh tokens expire after 6 months, after which the user must re-authorize.

evidence.quote: Once you use a refresh token, that refresh token and the old user access token

blockers.title: redirect_uri mismatch
blockers.symptom: GitHub shows a redirect_uri mismatch error instead of the consent screen.
blockers.fix: Register every environment's callback (up to 10) and pass the matching redirect_uri explicitly; without it GitHub uses the first registered URL. Avoid wildcard matching unless you control every subdomain/path.

evidence.quote: If you do not specify a `redirect_uri`, the first callback URL will be used.

blockers.title: Device flow errors: device_flow_disabled or slow_down
blockers.symptom: Polling returns device_flow_disabled, or repeated slow_down errors.
blockers.fix: Tick "Enable Device Flow" in app settings; respect the returned interval (default 5s) and add 5s after each slow_down. Restart the flow after 900 seconds.

evidence.quote: Device flow has not been enabled in the app's settings.

blockers.title: Rate limits hit by an agent doing many API calls
blockers.symptom: 403/429 with x-ratelimit-remaining: 0, or secondary rate limit errors when creating content quickly.
blockers.fix: User tokens share the user's 5,000 req/hour; installation tokens start at 5,000/hour and scale with repos and users (15,000 on GitHub Enterprise Cloud). Prefer installation tokens for bulk work, use conditional requests, and keep content creation under 80/minute and 500/hour.

evidence.quote: GitHub Apps authenticating with an installation access token use the installation's minimum rate limit

blockers.title: Paid Marketplace listing blocked
blockers.symptom: Cannot add a paid plan or request verification.
blockers.fix: Transfer the app to an organization, require 2FA for the org, verify a domain, complete Publisher Verification, and reach 100 installations (GitHub App) / 200 users (OAuth App). Launch as a free listing or off-Marketplace first.

evidence.quote: your app must be owned by an organization that is a verified publisher.

Exact current button label for generating a client secret on a GitHub App settings page (we used 'Generate a new client secret') is not stated in the docs we read; private-key labels are now 'Key pairs' > 'New key'.
Marketplace submit button label differs across docs: 'Request publish' (Submitting your listing) vs 'Submit for review' (Drafting a listing).
The 'Advanced' page location for changing GitHub App visibility is inferred from Modifying a GitHub App registration; the exact control label was not captured.

The 'Deciding when to build a GitHub App' page still says OAuth app tokens do not expire until revoked, while the OAuth App creation page says expiring tokens are enabled by default for new apps; behavior for existing OAuth Apps is opt-in.

verificationLog.check: OAuth Apps allow only one callback URL (commonly repeated advice)
verificationLog.detail: Current 'Creating an OAuth app' doc says you can enter up to 10 callback URLs via 'Add callback URL'. The older 'GitHub Apps allow multiple, OAuth Apps one' distinction no longer holds; both allow up to 10.

'Creating an OAuth app' now shows 'Expire user access tokens' enabled by default (8h access token, 6-month refresh token). The 'Deciding when to build a GitHub App' page still states OAuth tokens do not expire until revoked, so GitHub's own docs are inconsistent; existing apps keep long-lived tokens unless switched.

verificationLog.check: GitHub App private key generated via 'Generate a private key' button
verificationLog.detail: Current docs describe app settings sidebar 'Key pairs' > 'New key' within a 'Credentials' section; the older single 'Generate a private key' button wording is outdated.

verificationLog.check: GitHub App user tokens expire after 8 hours with 6-month refresh tokens
verificationLog.detail: Refreshing user access tokens: expires_in always 28800, refresh_token_expires_in 15897600; 'Expire user authorization tokens' strongly recommended. The page also labels expiring tokens as an optional feature subject to change.

verificationLog.check: No GitHub review required to make a GitHub App public
verificationLog.detail: Making a GitHub App public or private and Registering a GitHub App describe visibility as a setting with no review; only Marketplace listing involves an onboarding expert review.

verificationLog.check: Org owners must approve OAuth apps
verificationLog.detail: Only when OAuth app access restrictions are enabled, which is the default for new organizations. Orgs without restrictions let any member-authorized OAuth app access private org resources. GitHub Apps are not subject to these policies but require owner/admin installation.

verificationLog.check: Marketplace verification required for all listings
verificationLog.detail: Publisher verification is only required for paid plans or the Marketplace badge; free listings need only the general listing requirements. Paid apps also need 100 installs (GitHub App) / 200 users (OAuth App).

verificationLog.check: PKCE support in GitHub web flow
verificationLog.detail: Generating a user access token lists code_challenge / code_challenge_method as strongly recommended; only S256 supported.
Submitting your listing for publication says only that an onboarding expert will reach out; no duration published. Community range 2-6 weeks recorded as unverified.
